comments.author: @aremoreequal
comments.text: The human brain is sort of made up from several smaller brains put together. Not only are there the different lobes that do things, but the cerebellum, and the basal ganglia, and there's evidence that the spinal cord itself has some memory with reflexes and such. So, with that running commentary that many of us have, that single primary voice that many (but allegidly not all) of us have, is that parts of our brain that are not as smart monitoring parts of the brain that are smarter? I recall on that documentary style show Superhumans, where a guy who was super-great at math said he "felt" the answers. People often "feel" the correct answers to things, they call it their "gut feeling." ("You have to follow your gut.") Walking, throwing a ball, catching a ball, etc. our brain is doing super complex calculations all the time just to keep us standing upright. I wonder if our brain is all these different pieces working together as a way of error checking everything.

comments.author: @DeliciousHoneyDewDew2
comments.text: I'm calling BS on AI risks. Here's why: experts are calling for regulations on LLMs, but there's a glaring silence on two critical fronts. First, the military use of AI, which holds immense potential for harm, seems to be off their radar. Second, humanoid robots capable of physical harm aren't getting the regulatory attention they deserve. And then there's the paradox of their worry about AI risks while actively pushing the boundaries towards AGI  and ASI. To me, it looks like a strategic move to draw attention to their work, boosting their personal profits and inflating the valuations of their startups. It's a selective focus that raises questions about the real motivations in AI development and regulation.
